text: I now give the floor to her excellency
Victoria Luise Halam, chair of the
delegation of New Zealand.
President, over the past week, we have
listened to leaders, ministers, and
representatives from every region of the
world. They have spoken of different
priorities and concerns. Yet, they have
also revealed how much we have in
common. We have been reminded that the
biggest challenges we face do not
respect national borders, and no
country, however large or powerful, can
address them alone.
It is clear we live in a more contested,
fragmented and volatile world.
The number of active conflicts in the
world has doubled in the past 20 years.
The number of conflict related deaths
has reached levels not seen in decades.
Fundamental norms governing state
behavior are being violated with
increasing impunity, contravening the UN
charter and other universally applicable
rules of international law. Core human
rights that protect the well-being and
dignity of our citizens are increasingly
being humanitarian needs are growing
faster than our collective ability to
meet them.
After decades of progress, hard one
development gains have slowed and it's
clear we will fail to meet most of the
sustainable development goals by their
2030 target.
Biodiversity loss and pollution are
impacting key natural resources in our
oceans.
Natural disasters and the glowing imp
growing impacts of our changing climate
are becoming more severe and more
visible.
In our region, these pressures are
already affecting the lives,
livelihoods, and long-term development
prospects.
All of this is of grave concern to New
Zealand, whose sovereignty, security,
and prosperity depends on a functioning
inclusive multilateral system grounded
in agreed rules and norms with the UN
charter at its center.
We regard the UN charter with its core
principles of sovereign equality of
states, territorial integrity, the
prohibition of the use of force and
respect for human rights as
irreplaceable.
We continue therefore to invest in the
United Nations and agreed international
rules as an exercise of our sovereignty
because we believe it is essential to
our interests
and indeed the interests of all
in the face of rising volatility. We
need the UN stabilizing influence and
global solutions more than ever.
President, over recent years, New
Zealand has spoken of the importance of
leadership.
New Zealand thanks Secretary General
Antonio Guterres for his service over
the past 10 years.
We thank you for your visits to the Blue
Pacific and for your attention to the
unique situation of Pacific Island
countries and other small island
developing states.
We thank you also for starting the
process of essential reform to put this
vital organization on a stronger and
more sustainable footing to deal with
the challenges of the next 80 years.
Your assignment has not been easy.
As we prepare to appoint the next
secretary general to lead the UN into
the next phase, we should be clear about
what this moment requires.
First and foremost, we call on the new
Secretary General to be a courageous
guardian of the UN charter and to assert
the UN's vital role on peace and
security.
The United Nations was created to save
succeeding generations from the scourge
of war.
It is ultimately the responsibility of
member states to prevent and resolve
conflicts.
We cannot outsource that responsibility.
But at the same time, we need a
secretary general who is active in
conflict prevention, mediation, and
peacemaking.
The Secretary General should never have
to ask permission or forgiveness for
acting to prevent or resolve conflict.
As a custodian of the UN Charter, you
have the right and the obligation to
speak up when its core norms are
breached.
We expect you to do so in an objective,
impartial, and consistent manner.
We will support you when you do.
So we ask you to be active in seeking an
end to the horrific conflict in Sudan.
You must be bold in pressing for a
sustainable and just end to Russia's
illegal invasion of Ukraine,
one that is consistent with Ukraine's
sovereignty and territorial integrity
and the core principles of the charter.
You must be determined in your efforts
to help alleviate the dire humanitarian
situation in Gaza.
We ask that you use your influence to
progress a fragile ceasefire into a
sustainable, durable peace.
And you must be resolute in preserving
conditions for a two-state solution.
You must take the initiative despite the
challenges and entrenched views to
achieve a just and lasting resolution
where Israel and Palestine can live side
by side within secure and clearly
defined borders.
We urge you to use your good offices to
secure a lasting end to hostilities in
the Persian Gulf and restore freedom of
navigation through the Straight of
Hummus,
which is a right guaranteed under
international law.
Of course, you cannot do this alone. For
our part as member states, we must
provide you with the tools, the
resources, and above all, the political
support to ensure you can play this role
effectively.
Parties to conflicts must engage with
you constructively and in good faith,
while global and regional partners with
influence must provide the necessary
incentive for the parties to do so.
The UN Security Council needs to fill
fulfill its responsibilities.
Permanent members in particular must act
in a manner consistent with their
special responsibilities under the
charter.
Too frequently has the veto or the
threat of the veto been abused to block
the council from fulfilling its
responsibilities
to the frustration and sometimes despair
of the global community.
Inevitably, the costs of this fa failure
are borne by those caught in conflict.
This assembly also has a legitimate and
necessary role to play in maintaining
peace and security
and we have been pleased to see it step
up on occasions when the security
council has been stymied from acting.
For our part, New Zealand will continue
to press for a more effective, credible,
transparent and representative Security
Council.
As a demonstration of our continued
commitment to collective security and
the UN charter, New Zealand is seeking a
seat on the UN Security Council for 2039
to 40.
We ask the next secretary general to
work with us to preserve the integrity
of the global disarmament framework,
particularly on weapons of mass
destruction.
The grave dangers of deterioration of
the global non-prololiferation regime
should alarm us all.
New Zealand was deeply disappointed at
the failure to reach consensus at this
year's nuclear non-prololiferation
review conference.
After three consecutive review
conference failures, we must do all we
can to preserve the health of the NPT
and indeed strengthen it.
This means tackling persistent
violations and cases of non-compliance.
Iran is not in compliance with its
nuclear safeguards obligations.
The DPRK's nuclear weapons and missile
programs continue to threaten its region
and beyond.
Halting the NPT's deterioration also in
requires concrete action from nuclear
weapon states to at long last chart a
path towards total verifiable and
irreversible nuclear disarmament.
We also call on you to safeguard the UN
convention on the law of the sea, the
constitution for the oceans, which
provides the framework within which all
activities in the oceans and seas must
be carried out.
Compliance with these universally
applicable rules is essential not only
for maintaining peace and security but
also for protecting prosperity and food
security given the ocean's vital role in
supporting trade.
Second, we call on the next secretary
general to provide strong leadership
across the UN's development and human
rights pillars.
The authors of the UN charter understood
that peace and security cannot be
sustained without creating the
conditions for member states to provide
their citizens with prosperity and the
full enjoyment of human rights.
With significant changes in the global
development cooperation landscape, we
ask you to ensure that the UN is clear
about where its comparative advantage
lies alongside the role of governments,
regional organizations, and
international financial institutions.
Citizens and donors expect the UN to
operate as one with agencies working
together through a strengthened resident
coordinator system.
We will work with you to ensure the UN
is more coordinated and focused on
strengthening local capacity and
partnerships to address a country's
development needs.
The UN development system must remain
relevant, responsive, and accessible to
all member states based on need rather
than size, income level, or location.
We welcome progress in advancing the
UN's multi-dimensional vulnerability
index and want to see further work to
ensure its practical application across
the multilateral development system.
In the face of contracting development
finance flows and increasing debt
levels, we need to ensure our ambitions
are matched by more sustainable and
predictable financing.
This will inevitably involve moving
beyond exclusive reliance on traditional
sources and approaches.
President, as Pacific Island Forum
leaders recently reaffirmed in Palao,
climate change remains the single
greatest threat to the livelihoods,
security, and well-being of Pacific
peoples.
While New Zealand will play its part,
our efforts will mean little in the
absence of determined action by the
world's major admitters.
Rising sea levels continue to threaten
the viability of many communities and
pose a threat to low-lying island
states, including some of our Pacific
neighbors.
The political declaration on sea level
rise endorsed this week is a potent
demonstration of the UN's ability to
address contemporary challenges
affecting its members.
We particularly welcome the
declaration's affirmation of the
preservation of maritime zones and the
presumption of continued statehood
notwithstanding sea level rise.
We also expect the new secretary general
to defend international humanitarian law
and international human rights law and
its institutions.
The promotion and protection of
universal and indivisible human rights
is fundamental to the world we live in
today and to a collective vision of our
future. Societies
in which citizens can enjoy their
universal human rights have a better
chance of avoiding the descent into
conflict that tragically impacts so many
across the world today.
Over the past decade, these norms have
often been under threat, sometimes
through neglect, sometimes through
deliberate and sustained attacks.
The rise of attacks on protected
individuals, including civilians and
humanitarian and medical personnel,
needs particular attention.
It is now 10 years since New Zealand
co-led the adoption of Security Council
resolution 2286 on healthcare and armed
conflict. Attacks on medical facilities
and personnel in violation of
international human humanitarian law
have grown exponentially worse since
then.
Few have been held accountable for these
flagrant violations of international
humanitarian law.
We ask you to help us reverse these
trends by drawing on the UN's unique
legitimacy to call out egregious and
systematic violations of these norms
wherever they may occur and whoever may
be perpetrating them and by providing
practical guidance and assistance to
help member states meet their
obligations.
Third, we ask the new secretary general
to maintain momentum and ambition on UN
reform.
Confidence in this institution depends
on its ability to deliver impact.
The next secretary general must work
with member states to chart an ambitious
vision for the next phase of reform
while ensuring implementation of the
decisions already taken.
At a time of multiple and overlapping
crises and growing constraints, we need
a United Nations that is focused on its
core tasks, disciplined and accountable.
One where every dollar delivers maximum
impact.
One that measures success
not by the number of mandates it creates
or the meetings it holds, but by the
difference it makes in people's lives.
Meeting this challenge means exercising
your powers to achieve the most impact
from the resources available. It means
demanding a culture of continuous
improvement, one that focuses on
effective implementation and results.
It means setting the highest standards
for performance within the secretariat
and holding staff accountable for
delivering.
In this regard, we ask you to
demonstrate independence in your senior
appointments.
New Zealand has never accepted the right
of any country to assert ownership of UN
positions by virtue of power or status.
We encourage Secretary General
candidates to commit publicly to making
senior appointments on the basis of
merit.
Reform is a joint responsibility. We as
member states must avoid the trap of
regarding reform as something that
others will deliver for us and instead
live up to our own responsibilities in
building the organization we need.
We cannot expect the UN to continue to
lurch on in a state of constant
financial crisis. Member states must
meet their financial obligations in
full, on time, and without conditions in
accordance with their obligations under
the charter.
We need to focus our attention on the
issues that really matter and that can
genuinely deliver benefits for our
citizens.
Resolution 80251 equips member states to
tackle the long-standing challenge of
mandate accumulation and overload.
It commits us all to take a more
disciplined approach to setting the
organization's priorities.
It provides the framework we need to
create a more focused, coherent, and
impactful UN.
Yet its success will depend on whether
we are willing to act differently.
If we aren't prepared to make the
necessary choices, we will be left with
an ever go growing set of
responsibilities
supported by an evershrinking pool of
resources
that will do nothing to strengthen
confidence in the UN's relevance and
effectiveness.
Reform begins with us. It requires
member states to make the decisions that
only member states can make.
That is the only way we can truly
achieve an organization that is fit to
meet the challenges that lie before us
and that our citizens need and expect.
Fourth, and finally, we urge the next
Secretary General to ensure that the UN
works for all states.
The sovereign equality of states is one
of the most central principles of the UN
charter. It must be central also to your
approach.
The fundamental premise of the United
Nations is that every state, regardless
of size or circumstance, has a stake in
shaping our shared future.
We also call on the president of the
general assembly to remain a steadfast
champion of the voices, prerogatives and
interests of the entire UN membership
across all pillars of its work.
The next secretary general's leadership
in these areas will be essential, but we
must also find it in ourselves to
demonstrate leadership.
Ultimately, the health relevance and
effectiveness of the United Nations
depends primarily on its members, not
its secretary general.
As member states, we must acknowledge
our role in the financial and legitimacy
crisis facing the UN.
We must ask whether we have the
collective will to change our behavior.
Do we have the discipline to focus our
attention and resources on the issues
that really matter to our citizens and
deliver impact to their lives?
Do we have the honesty to admit what is
working and what is not?
Do we have the will to invest in the
multilateral system both politically and
financially to enable it to deliver
results where we can truly make a
difference?
coupled with the courage to make bold
and consequent decisions on UN reform
that can deliver a more effective
organization.
Collective action has changed the course
of global challenges before.
These achievements were not inevitable.
They were the result of political
leadership, persistence, and a
willingness to work together despite
differences to build understanding and
compromise.
The most fundamental step we can all
take to revive this organization is to
unequivocally recommmit ourselves both
in words and deeds to the principles
that the charter requires us to follow
in our relations with other states.
respect for sovereignty, international
law, the pursuit of dialogue and
cooperation, and the peaceful settlement
of disputes.
At a time when conflict is rising, trust
is eroding, and geopolitical competition
is intensifying,
we should not conclude that
multilateralism has failed.
We should conclude that it is needed
more than ever. Thank you.
I thank the chair of delegation of New
Zealand.
